details:
**Compatibilism**
The view that free will can coexist with determinism, usually by defining freedom as acting on one's own desires without external coercion. Hume, John Stuart Mill, and Daniel Dennett are associated with it, and it appears in nearly every question on this topic.

**Determinism**
The view that every event is the necessary result of prior causes, so there is only one possible course of events. It is the usual opposite of free will, and incompatibilists hold that the two cannot both be true.

**Frankfurt cases and the Principle of Alternate Possibilities (PAP)**
Harry Frankfurt's thought experiments, in which a hidden controller would force a person to act in a certain way (for example, to vote for a particular candidate) but never has to step in because the person chooses that action anyway. They are meant to refute the PAP, which says a person is morally responsible only if they could have done otherwise. Frankfurt also proposed a "mesh" or hierarchical theory in which freedom means one's first-order desires agree with one's second-order desires.

**Alvin Plantinga's Free Will Defense**
Plantinga's reply to the logical problem of evil. It argues that God may be unable to create free creatures who never sin, because of "transworld depravity," the possibility that every creature God could create would freely do wrong in at least one situation.

**Daniel Dennett's Elbow Room: The Varieties of Free Will Worth Wanting**
Dennett's 1984 compatibilist book, based on his John Locke Lectures at Oxford. It discusses the fear of "sphexishness," named after the Sphex digger wasp, which mechanically repeats the same behavior when disturbed, as a picture of mindless determined behavior.

**Metaphysical libertarianism**
The incompatibilist view that free will exists and determinism is therefore false, so agents can choose between multiple genuinely open outcomes. Roderick Chisholm defended it by distinguishing "agent causation," in which a person directly causes an action, from ordinary "event causation."

**Laplace's demon**
Pierre-Simon Laplace's imagined intellect that knows the position and momentum of every particle in the universe, and so could predict the entire future and reconstruct the entire past. It is a classic illustration of how determinism seems to rule out free will.

**Schopenhauer's On the Freedom of the Will**
Arthur Schopenhauer's prize essay arguing that individual actions are strictly determined by motives, since only one thing can be done at any given moment. Building on Kant, he held that phenomena (things as they appear) lack freedom, while freedom belongs only to the noumenal will (things in themselves).

**Augustine's De Libero Arbitrio (On Free Choice of the Will)**
Augustine's dialogue with Evodius, which discusses eternal and temporal law and traces evil to the misuse of free will. Augustine held that sin burdens the will and that true freedom is restored through God's grace.

**Divine foreknowledge and theological fatalism**
The problem that if God infallibly knows our future actions, we seem unable to do otherwise. Boethius answered in The Consolation of Philosophy that God is outside time and sees all events at once, like someone viewing a road from a mountain, and theists such as Richard Swinburne also argue that the two are compatible.

**Molinism and "middle knowledge"**
The view of the Jesuit Luis de Molina that God knows counterfactuals of freedom, meaning what any free creature would freely choose in any situation. This lets God's providence coexist with genuine human freedom.

**Henri Bergson's Time and Free Will**
Bergson's doctoral thesis (French title Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience). It attacks Kant's view that freedom exists only outside space and time and defends freedom through Bergson's idea of lived time, or "duration."

**Epicurean clinamen ("the swerve")**
The Epicurean doctrine, described in Lucretius's On the Nature of Things, that atoms falling through the void sometimes swerve unpredictably, which breaks the chain of causes and makes room for free will. Stephen Greenblatt's book The Swerve takes its title from this idea.

**William James**
The pragmatist who argued in "The Dilemma of Determinism" that it is reasonable to believe in free will even without conclusive evidence. He is also credited with a "two-stage" model of free will, in which random possibilities are generated first and then chosen among by the will.

**Libet's experiments**
Benjamin Libet's neuroscience experiments found that a "readiness potential" (Bereitschaftspotential) in the brain appears before subjects report being aware of deciding to move. They are often cited as evidence against conscious free will. In earlier philosophy, Hume called the question of liberty and necessity "the most contentious question of metaphysics."
